# The composition fixtures, and the `wac` pin

`wac` is the pinned composition tool. These fixtures are its witness: a tool pinned with nothing
exercising it is a pin nobody has tested.

## Provenance, read from the tools rather than recalled

```
wac-cli      0.12.0          installed with `cargo install wac-cli --locked`
wasm-tools   1.258.0         assembles the sockets; `component wit` reads the composed worlds
```

`compose.sh` prints both versions before composing, so a regeneration records what it actually used
rather than what this block says. The child is the committed `../asynclift/receipt/component.wasm`, whose
own provenance is in [that README](../asynclift/README.md).

## Why `wac` and not `wasm-tools compose`

`wasm-tools compose` still exists in 1.258.0 and prints, on every invocation:

```
WARNING: `wasm-tools compose` has been deprecated.
Please use `wac` instead.
```

A committed, reproducible artefact should not be built by a tool that tells you to stop using it. **And
the two disagree**, which is how this fixture came to exist:

| socket imports | `wasm-tools compose` | `wac plug` |
|---|---|---|
| a **bare** world-level function | `error: no dependencies of component were found` | composes |
| an **interface** instance | composes | composes |

I measured the first row with `compose` and read it as a property of *composition*, which briefly cost
[#862](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/burroughs/issues/862) a plan to add a second `receipt` guest with an
interface-shaped export. `wac` composes the existing guest as it is, so no second guest exists and every
reading and hash taken against `receipt/` keeps its subject. **An absence claim is only as wide as its
search**, and a search over one deprecated tool is not a search over composition.

## What is here

| path | what it is |
|---|---|
| `parent-supplied.wat` / `.wasm` | a socket whose one import is exactly what `receipt/` exports |
| `parent-missing.wat` / `.wasm` | the same socket plus one import nothing can supply |
| `composed-supplied.wasm` | `wac plug` of the receipt guest into the first socket |
| `composed-missing.wasm` | the same, into the second — **`wac` exits 0 producing this** |
| `compose.sh` | regenerates all four; run deliberately, out of CI |

The witness is `TestWacSatisfiesThePluggedImportAndLeavesTheRest`, which reads the **committed** composed
bytes with this engine's own decoder. `wac` is not in CI and does not need to be: commit the tool's
output, never depend on the tool at test time — the same rule as `asynclift/`'s guests and readings.

## Reproducibility, measured

**All four committed `.wasm` files rebuild byte-for-byte**, from a clean `git worktree` at
`/tmp/repro-compose` — a different absolute path from the tree that produced them, so path-dependence
would have shown as a mismatch. `git status` in that worktree reported **nothing changed**:

```
parent-supplied.wasm     2c477fff7a3afb6f929fe1eaf5895c2cb2431837bfd11d94843f301b65f0dd24   MATCH
parent-missing.wasm      4c450678485348601776d36ee0645d40767c3c7205a2552942ade235ee080215   MATCH
composed-supplied.wasm   aad1cb8f711a359562c602bb6b15704ff47e13b8b0846ed91bc0f35cf6d50981   MATCH
composed-missing.wasm    8d84ec379b156bef9b08c4affe4b58ac963f4ea3ed909fbac181f4b39bac3ebb   MATCH
```

**Run because `wac` is new here and had not been shown deterministic.** A composer embeds one component
inside another and could reasonably carry a path, a timestamp, or an unordered map into the output —
which is exactly what this check exists to catch, and what it caught for the guests next door when a
crate rename silently changed their bytes.

**This table has a dependency the one next door does not.** Its input, `../asynclift/receipt/component.wasm`
(`4c0f63f9…`), is itself a committed artefact, so these four reproduce *given* that the child does.
That the child reproduces is established by [asynclift's own table](../asynclift/README.md), and the
hash above is the one recorded there — so the chain is checked end to end rather than assumed at the
join. Recorded here rather than folded into that table because these artefacts live in this directory
and are regenerated by this script.

## The two things the witness asserts, and why neither is the obvious one

**Not "the composition succeeded".** `wac plug` **exits 0 for both sockets**, including the one whose
dependency it could not satisfy. The status channel cannot tell them apart, so the check reads the
composed artefact's **payload** — which imports it still has.

**Not "zero imports".** `receipt/` has its own host imports, `tick` and `note`, and composition correctly
leaves them for the host to supply. A zero-import expectation would **fail on a correct composition**. So
the assertion is directional: the *plugged* import is gone, the *child's own* imports remain.

```
composed-supplied:  tick, note                 <- `run` satisfied by the plug
composed-missing:   missing, tick, note        <- `missing` outstanding, wac said nothing
```

## A measurement error worth not repeating

The first reading of these worlds counted `(import` lines in `wasm-tools print` output at any
indentation. `wac` **nests** both components, so the nested socket's own import declaration is still in
the printed text and is supposed to be — the count matched it and read as *"the plugged import
survived"*, which would have confirmed the wrong conclusion by a second route. The worlds are read with a
parser instead: `wasm-tools component wit` in the script, and `Load` plus `c.Imports` in the witness.

## The socket's shape is forced, not chosen

Each of these was found by a refusal, and `parent-supplied.wat` records them at the line they apply to:
the import must be **async** to match `receipt/`'s async export; an async `canon lower` requires a
**`memory`** canonopt; and the core import's flat signature is `(param i32 i32) (result i32)` — the
argument plus a **return pointer** — not `(param i32) (result i32)`.
